MVLM: Template-Free Tracking via Vision–Language Margin Confidence
and Memory-Gated Tracking
Dae-Hyeon Park
Mina Baek
Jeong-Hun Ha
Chan-Seop Park
Jamshidjon Ganiev
Seung-Hwan Bae*
Inha University, Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Vision and Learning Lab.
{saintPalite2221,dkdend123,jhha,pcs1728,jamshid24}@inha.edu,
shbae@inha.ac.kr
https://mvlm-tft.github.io
Abstract
We introduce a new template-free tracking paradigm based
solely on natural language, capable of tracking an arbitrary
object and seamlessly switching to a new target without
box initialization. Our key idea is to localize an object via
vision-language (VL) correlation. However, using the cor-
relation alone is brittle under large search regions due to
spatial uncertainty and ambiguous VL saliency. To resolve
these, we propose MVLM, a memory-based vision-language
margin confidence that integrates vision–language corre-
lation, encoder prediction, and temporal memory. MVLM
dynamically gates the search region—switching between
compact ROI (Region of Interest) search and global re-
localization—to reduce spatial uncertainty. Theoretically,
we derive bounds that connect the MVLM score to tracking
probability, characterizing mis-localization within ROI and
ROI-exclusion probabilities. Through extensive evaluation,
we validate our theorems and achieve state-of-the-art per-
formance on several benchmarks (TNL2K, LaSOT, OTB99,
and MGIT) using only language guidance.
1. Introduction
Template-free (TF) tracking with natural language elimi-
nates the need for visual templates or box initialization, al-
lowing a tracker to follow arbitrary objects and seamlessly
switch to a new target by updating the text description.
This is beneficial for open-world and interactive scenarios,
where the user may not have an initial bounding box and
the target can change on the fly. Although the earlier works
[23, 26, 30, 38] state language-based tracking, they exploit
object templates as an input to a tracker. In contrast, our
approach eliminates visual object templates completely, re-

lying solely on vision-language correlation as the semantic
anchor.
A natural approach is to localize the object by measur-
ing the correlation between vision features (from a search
image) and a language query. However, correlation-alone
tracking is unstable under broad search regions: spatial un-
certainty grows with the area to scan, and vision–language
(VL) saliency becomes ambiguous in the presence of dis-
tractors, occlusions, or appearance shifts. As a result, track-
ers that rely only on instantaneous VL correlation tend to
mislocalize or lose the target when the search region is
large. Therefore, recent transformer-based object trackers
[3–8, 13, 15, 31–34, 36] employ local ROI search for re-
stricting the search region around the tracked object pre-
dicted at a past frame. From these observations, the main
problem of TF tracking can be transformed into learn-
ing distinctive saliency from vision-language correlation
and determining object search regions around an object or
global image region according to tracking and language
guidance.
To resolve these, we propose memory-based vision-
language confidence (MVLM) by incorporating three com-
plementary features: (i) a VL correlation margin that sepa-
rates the best-matching hypothesis from its nearest competi-
tors, (ii) the encoder’s output statistics that capture local vi-
sual evidence, and (iii) a lightweight temporal memory that
stabilizes decisions across frames. We then exploit MVLM
to gate the search strategy: when MVLM confidence is
high, the tracker restricts itself to a compact ROI around the
current estimate; when confidence drops, it triggers global
re-localization over the whole image. This memory-gated
tracking reduces spatial uncertainty without sacrificing re-
coverability after failures or during target switching.
